lessons.title: Welcome to Freight Brokerage Training

video_storyboard.heading: Welcome to Freight Brokerage Training
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Welcome to Freight Brokerage Training.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: A freight broker arranges transportation rather than physically carrying freight. During this course you will follow a fictional shipment from a shipper's request through carrier payment. Keep a separate document for every quote, approval, rate confirmation, status update, and invoice. That habit is not busywork: a defensible transaction record is one of the most important brokerage controls.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: Imagine that a manufacturer asks for a truck tomorrow but has not provided pallet weight or delivery hours. The correct first step is to request missing details, not to guess a price. At the end of training, your portfolio should prove that you can gather those details and coordinate the move.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Create a training folder named Brokerage Practice and add folders for Prospects, Quotes, Carriers, Active Loads, Delivered Loads and Accounting.

lessons.title: Understanding the Freight Transportation Industry

video_storyboard.heading: Understanding the Freight Transportation Industry
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Understanding the Freight Transportation Industry.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: A typical supply chain connects producers, warehouses, distributors, retail locations and final recipients. The shipper initiates the transportation need; the consignee receives it; a motor carrier supplies equipment and driver capacity. Warehousing and transportation decisions interact: missed appointments can cause storage costs, stockouts or production interruptions.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A Chicago manufacturer loads pallets for a Dallas distribution center. The broker confirms pickup access in Chicago, delivery appointment in Dallas, freight weight and equipment specifications. Even when both facilities are open, a narrow appointment window can change which carrier is suitable.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Map one shipment through shipper, broker, carrier and consignee. Record the information each party must exchange.

lessons.title: What Is a Freight Broker?

video_storyboard.heading: What Is a Freight Broker?
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to What Is a Freight Broker?.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: A property broker arranges or offers to arrange transportation by authorized motor carriers for compensation. Brokers differ from carriers, which physically transport property, and freight forwarders, which take on distinct responsibilities. A broker should never represent itself as the actual carrier when it is arranging the truck.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: If the shipper agrees to $2,400 and an authorized carrier agrees to $1,950, the broker's gross profit is $450 and gross margin is 18.75%. Those amounts are not net earnings because office costs, software, claims, financing and labor remain. The broker must also verify the carrier before tendering the load.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Describe the parties and calculate gross profit and margin on the Chicago-to-Dallas shipment.

lessons.title: How a Freight Brokerage Makes Money

video_storyboard.heading: How a Freight Brokerage Makes Money
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to How a Freight Brokerage Makes Money.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: A broker generally earns the spread between the amount charged to the customer and the amount owed to the motor carrier. Gross profit equals customer revenue minus carrier transportation cost. Gross margin measures gross profit as a percentage of customer revenue, while markup measures gross profit as a percentage of carrier cost. Mixing up the two produces pricing mistakes.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: For a $2,000 carrier buy rate, a 20% markup creates a $2,400 sell rate and a 16.67% margin. To earn a true 20% gross margin, divide $2,000 by 0.80: the required sell rate is $2,500. Accessorial costs can reduce profit if they are not approved and passed through appropriately.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Calculate a quote using both 20% markup and 20% margin, then reconcile the difference.

lessons.title: Freight Broker vs. Freight Broker Agent

video_storyboard.heading: Freight Broker vs. Freight Broker Agent
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Freight Broker vs. Freight Broker Agent.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: An independent brokerage operates using its own authority, security arrangements, customer agreements and compliance program. A broker agent works under another brokerage's authority and usually receives a negotiated share of gross profit. An agent still needs to follow the brokerage's screening, contracting, security and customer processes.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: If an agent brings a load earning $500 gross profit and receives a 60% split, the agent earns $300 before any separate contractual deductions. The brokerage retains $200 to support authority, technology, insurance, accounting and supervision. Compare the split alongside access to systems, liability allocation and payment timing, not just the headline percentage.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Build a table comparing startup cost, authority, billing, control and commission for independent brokerage versus agency.

lessons.title: A Day in the Life of a Freight Broker

video_storyboard.heading: A Day in the Life of a Freight Broker
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to A Day in the Life of a Freight Broker.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: A broker's workday is a sequence of time-sensitive commitments. Begin by reviewing active loads and overnight exceptions; confirm today's pickups and deliveries; respond to shipper requests; source and vet carriers; update stakeholders; then reconcile PODs and billing documents. Prospecting remains necessary even on busy operating days.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: At 8 a.m. two loads are late, one pickup has no confirmed truck and three customers request quotes. Resolve safety and service exposures first, secure the unassigned pickup, then issue researched quotes. Document the reason for each exception and its next owner so the problem does not disappear between shifts.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Build a priority list for five hypothetical loads and three customer requests.

lessons.title: Choosing Your Business Model

video_storyboard.heading: Choosing Your Business Model
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Choosing Your Business Model.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: A generalist brokerage offers many equipment types and lanes but faces broader competition and operational complexity. A niche brokerage focuses on an industry, equipment type or geographic corridor. An independent agent model lowers some setup burdens while leaving the agent dependent on the host broker's contract, permissions and back office.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A beginner with existing food-manufacturer contacts might target Midwest dry van lanes before attempting refrigerated produce or oversize machinery. Narrow specialization helps develop rate knowledge and a vetted carrier network. A clear niche does not prohibit other shipments; it prioritizes sales effort and operating competence.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Select a niche, three target lanes and two types of customers you will deliberately decline at launch.

lessons.title: Creating Your Business Plan

video_storyboard.heading: Creating Your Business Plan
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Creating Your Business Plan.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: A useful brokerage plan identifies the target shipper, service problem, expected gross profit per load, startup expense, cash reserves and repeatable sales activity. Revenue projections should use assumptions that can be tested: loads per customer per week, close rate, carrier buy rate and collection terms.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: Assume two customers each tender three loads weekly and average gross profit is $350. That is six loads and $2,100 weekly gross profit before overhead, not guaranteed cash flow. Test what happens if a customer pauses shipments or if average buy rates rise.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Prepare conservative, expected and optimistic 90-day projections with explicit assumptions.

video_storyboard.heading: Establishing Your Business
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Establishing Your Business.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Business entity formation and federal brokerage authority are separate decisions. An LLC or corporation may provide business structure and administrative benefits, but it does not by itself authorize brokerage activity. Maintain consistent legal names, EIN details, banking records, business address and contracting information across filings.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A brokerage registers an LLC with its state and opens a business bank account. It still cannot broker regulated interstate motor carrier transportation solely because the LLC exists. The operator must secure the applicable federal registration and financial responsibility before operating.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Create a checklist for entity filing, EIN, bank account, bookkeeping, registrations and professional advisers.

video_storyboard.heading: Building Your Brand and Business Identity
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Building Your Brand and Business Identity.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Professional branding tells a shipper what you arrange, the lanes you understand and how you communicate. Make the broker role explicit. A credible brand emphasizes reliable tracking, responsive support and vetted carrier access rather than unverifiable promises of being the cheapest.

video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: Compare two introductions: 'We move anything anywhere at the lowest cost' offers little credibility. 'We arrange Midwest-to-Texas dry van loads with appointment coordination and proactive delivery updates' gives a defined service promise that can be measured.

lessons.title: Planning Startup Costs and Cash Reserves

video_storyboard.heading: Planning Startup Costs and Cash Reserves
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Planning Startup Costs and Cash Reserves.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Startup expenses include operating authority filings, financial security premiums or trust funding, software, communications, marketing and professional support. Working capital is separate: a broker may need to pay a carrier before collecting from the shipper. Growth in load count can create a cash shortage even while gross profit rises.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A broker owes carriers $12,000 this week but will not collect $15,000 of customer invoices for 30 days. That timing gap requires liquidity or an agreed financing arrangement. A factoring fee may improve timing but reduce net profit.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Create a startup budget separating one-time costs, monthly overhead and a carrier-payment reserve.

video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Designing Your Brokerage Workflow.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: A shipment should move through clear stages: lead, qualified customer, tender received, rate quoted, tender accepted, carrier approved, booked, picked up, in transit, delivered, invoiced and settled. Each transition has a required verification or document. Never treat 'carrier found' as equivalent to 'carrier approved.'

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A coordinator sees a carrier's name on a load board. The load should remain in sourcing until authority, identity and coverage checks pass. Once accepted, save the rate confirmation and contact details in the load record before dispatch.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Draw your workflow and identify one stop/go control for customer credit, carrier approval and payment release.

lessons.title: Federal vs. State Regulatory Requirements

video_storyboard.heading: Federal vs. State Regulatory Requirements
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Federal vs. State Regulatory Requirements.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Federal property-broker registration is administered by FMCSA; state-level entity, tax and local business rules are separate. Some commodities, shipping modes or activities involve additional specialized rules. Training should start with ordinary U.S. domestic property brokerage and clearly flag activities that require professional or legal review.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A company incorporated in Illinois wants to arrange interstate truckloads. Its Illinois registration does not substitute for FMCSA authority. It should also check local tax, business and contract obligations rather than assuming federal registration covers everything.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Write a responsibility matrix for FMCSA, state entity registration, taxation and professional insurance advice.

lessons.title: Obtaining Freight Broker Operating Authority

video_storyboard.heading: Obtaining Freight Broker Operating Authority
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Obtaining Freight Broker Operating Authority.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Before applying, confirm the registered legal business name, contact information and business classification. Follow FMCSA's current registration process, monitor the application status and verify that required process-agent and financial-security filings are accepted. Do not present application submission as equivalent to active authority.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: An applicant submits registration paperwork but the surety bond is not yet effective. The applicant should not begin brokering regulated shipments based solely on a receipt or pending registration number. The status must show authority is effective.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap

video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to BOC-3 and Process Agents.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: The BOC-3 filing designates agents authorized to receive legal process for the registrant. It is not cargo insurance and does not replace a broker's surety bond or trust fund. Use an appropriate process-agent provider and verify that the required filing is present in official records.

video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A new broker purchases a BOC-3 service but never confirms filing acceptance. When another compliance document is delayed, the owner learns that the application remains incomplete. Create a check-and-record routine instead of relying on emailed purchase receipts.

lessons.title: BMC-84 Surety Bond vs. BMC-85 Trust

video_storyboard.heading: BMC-84 Surety Bond vs. BMC-85 Trust
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to BMC-84 Surety Bond vs. BMC-85 Trust.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Federal property brokers generally must maintain $75,000 financial security through a BMC-84 surety bond or a qualifying BMC-85 trust arrangement. The bond usually requires a premium and underwriting; the trust requires qualifying security assets. Effective January 16, 2026, financial-responsibility providers and qualifying trust assets are subject to updated FMCSA rules.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A broker secures a BMC-84 bond with a $75,000 penal amount. The broker does not pay the full $75,000 as a routine premium; the quoted premium depends on underwriting. By contrast, an eligible trust arrangement involves qualifying assets securing the required amount. If available security drops below $75,000 and is not replenished within seven calendar days, authority may be suspended.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Compare hypothetical bond premiums with the liquidity effect of funding a trust and review the current FMCSA overview.

lessons.title: Broker Records, Contracts and Transparency

video_storyboard.heading: Broker Records, Contracts and Transparency
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Broker Records, Contracts and Transparency.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Under 49 CFR 371.3, a broker must keep a record of each transaction for three years. Required items include consignor identity, originating carrier information, bill-of-lading or freight-bill identification, broker compensation and freight-charge collection/payment details. Parties to the brokered transaction have record-review rights. Distinguish existing rules from proposed transparency amendments.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: For a shipment with freight bill FB-104, record the shipper, carrier registration details, amount charged, compensation, carrier payment and dates. Organize these in a retrievable file even if the transportation-management system stores them in separate screens.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Create a transaction-record checklist using the current text of 49 CFR 371.3 and reconcile it to a model load.

video_storyboard.heading: Maintaining Compliance After Launch
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Maintaining Compliance After Launch.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Compliance continues after the authority becomes active. Monitor operating status and financial security, keep legal names and records consistent, review service agreements and avoid accepting specialized freight outside the brokerage's capability. video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: Your bond provider sends a notice of nonrenewal. Do not wait for a shipper to discover an authority problem. Contact the provider immediately, document any replacement filing, and verify official status before tendering new freight.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Create a calendar for weekly authority checks, monthly account reconciliation and quarterly contract reviews.

video_storyboard.heading: Understanding Freight Characteristics
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Understanding Freight Characteristics.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: A useful tender specifies commodity, pieces or pallets, total gross weight, dimensions, packaging, stackability, special handling and pickup/delivery constraints. A vague commodity description may hide reefer requirements, weight restrictions or loading equipment needs. Ask for accurate data before offering an equipment or price commitment.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: 'Twenty pallets of packaged goods' is insufficient if the shipper has not provided total weight or pallet height. A load of 20 pallets weighing 45,000 pounds may have very different capacity requirements than 20 pallets weighing 10,000 pounds.

video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Create a complete intake form and identify five missing details from a vague load request.

lessons.title: Dry Van Freight

video_storyboard.heading: Dry Van Freight
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Dry Van Freight.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Dry vans are enclosed trailers used for many general commodities that do not require active temperature control. Trailer interior dimensions, door opening, floor capacity and equipment availability vary, so exact requirements must be verified with the carrier. Confirm loading method, seal procedure and whether the shipper requires swing doors or specific trailer conditions.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A customer tenders palletized boxed household products and asks for a 53-foot dry van. Before booking, verify gross weight, pallet height, dock loading compatibility and any cargo securement requirements. The broker should not infer that every trailer can accommodate every pallet arrangement.

video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Write a dry van quote request that includes commodity, total weight, trailer length and appointment details.

video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Refrigerated and Temperature-Controlled Freight.

video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Refrigerated shipments require documented temperature and product instructions, including whether equipment should be precooled and whether continuous operation is needed. video_storyboard.narration: A shipper requests chilled dairy but the tender lacks a temperature range. The broker must obtain the exact instructions before confirmation. If a reefer unit alarms in transit, notify the carrier and shipper promptly, capture temperature evidence and coordinate the next step.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Flatbed, step deck and removable gooseneck trailers solve different height and loading requirements. video_storyboard.heading: LTL Freight and Freight Classification
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to LTL Freight and Freight Classification.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Less-than-truckload shipments share trailer space with other customers' freight. Pricing often depends on origin, destination, weight, pallet dimensions, freight classification and service accessorials. NMFC classification rules changed in 2025 for many commodities; do not reuse a historical class without checking the current item and density requirements.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A shrink-wrapped pallet measures 48 by 40 by 60 inches and weighs 500 pounds. Its volume is 80,000/1,728, or about 55.56 cubic feet; its density is about 9 pounds per cubic foot. That density may inform classification but does not independently determine the correct class for every commodity.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Calculate density for three pallet sizes and research the applicable current NMFC item.

video_storyboard.heading: Understanding Freight Supply and Demand
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Understanding Freight Supply and Demand.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Truckload rates respond to the balance between shippers needing capacity and carriers offering it. Harvest seasons, holidays, severe weather, fuel prices and regional manufacturing cycles can shift that balance. A quoted lane price is a time-specific estimate, not an assurance that a truck will accept the load.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A produce market suddenly requires many reefers at the same time that regional trucks are scarce. An old rate from last month may no longer secure service. Recheck available capacity and give the shipper a price with a valid-until time.

video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Write a market update identifying two demand factors and two capacity factors for a lane.

lessons.title: What Is a Freight Lane?

video_storyboard.heading: What Is a Freight Lane?
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to What Is a Freight Lane?.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: A freight lane is a recurring origin-destination pattern. Lane pricing depends on mileage, geographic access, directional freight balance and the carrier's ability to find the next load. Deadhead is unpaid travel to pickup or repositioning; it can make a short haul unprofitable.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A carrier sits 120 miles from your shipper and would run 600 loaded miles. The carrier effectively travels 720 miles before the next load, so dividing the quoted buy rate only by loaded miles understates its operating exposure. This affects negotiation and truck availability.

video_storyboard.heading: Practice and next action
video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Compare two fictional carriers with different deadhead and loaded-mile totals.

video_storyboard.heading: Using Load Boards and Market Intelligence
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Using Load Boards and Market Intelligence.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: A load board is a capacity-matching tool, not a substitute for carrier screening. Compare equipment, pickup date, lane, postings, historical rate trends and source credibility. Rates published on a board may reflect asking prices or historical data rather than completed transactions.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: Three carriers quote $1,800, $1,950 and $2,200 for the same lane. Before choosing the cheapest, verify that each quote includes the same equipment, appointment timing and accessorial terms and that each carrier passes compliance screening.

video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap

video_storyboard.heading: Calculating Freight Transportation Costs
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Calculating Freight Transportation Costs.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: A carrier's price generally reflects time, distance, fuel, empty miles, tolls, labor, equipment utilization and service demands. Brokers should use these drivers to understand bids, not to assume they know each carrier's exact expenses. Accessorials such as detention and extra stops must be captured in the original request.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: Two shipments travel the same 500 miles, but one has a six-hour warehouse delay and an extra stop. Their transportation costs are not necessarily equal. Record stops and appointment windows in the tender so a quoted rate is comparable and enforceable.

video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Estimate cost drivers for a sample 500-mile haul with one additional stop.

video_storyboard.heading: Creating Profitable Shipper Quotes
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Creating Profitable Shipper Quotes.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Start with a qualified carrier buy estimate, add a risk allowance and determine the required gross margin. A quote should state origin, destination, dates, equipment, commodity assumptions, included stops and excluded accessorials. A low sell rate that cannot purchase reliable capacity is not a workable quote.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: With a $1,950 carrier cost and 20% target gross margin, the minimum sell rate before other costs is $1,950/0.8, or $2,437.50. Quoting $2,100 might win a customer but leaves only $150 gross profit and may not justify the exposure.

video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap
video_storyboard.narration: Build a written quote with a target 20% gross margin and clear expiration time.

video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Spot Rates, Contract Rates and Pricing Strategy.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Spot pricing addresses an individual shipment; contract pricing covers recurring needs under agreed rules. Contract freight benefits from volume predictability but can expose the broker to market-rate changes. Define minimum volume, fuel treatment, rate-review triggers and service parameters before committing to repeated loads.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A shipper offers three weekly loads for six months. The broker should not blindly use today's cheapest spot rate for a fixed six-month commitment. Evaluate seasonal capacity, carrier commitments and how surcharges or exceptional costs will be handled.

video_storyboard.visual: Checklist illustration and recap

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: An ideal shipper profile describes a real freight need you can serve reliably. Segment prospects by industry, equipment, recurring lanes, shipment frequency, buying process and service issues. A manufacturer that loads multiple dry vans weekly is very different from an individual moving household goods.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A broker specializing in Midwest-to-Texas dry van traffic looks for packaging manufacturers and regional distributors rather than calling every business in the phone book. The company can describe a service commitment for appointment updates and vetted carriers that matches those accounts.

video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold

video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Research companies that manufacture, import, distribute or wholesale physical goods. Public industrial directories, company websites, trade groups and referrals can identify facilities. Check the actual business and its shipping locations before contacting it; company headquarters is not always the pickup facility.

video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A food manufacturer lists corporate headquarters in Chicago but ships from a nearby distribution center. A useful prospect record includes the shipping facility and likely mode, not merely the corporate address. Research a relevant operations contact and prepare a question about the company's transportation process.

video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Building a Prospecting Database.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: A CRM should support follow-up, not become a list of unverified names. Capture business, contact role, email, phone, shipping location, target lanes, last contact, next action, service fit and lead stage. Keep factual notes separate from assumptions and do not retain unnecessary personal information.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: Two prospects both request a rate, but one ships weekly and one needs a one-time pickup. Mark the first as a potential recurring opportunity and schedule a specific follow-up. If a decision maker asks not to be contacted, respect the request and update the record.

video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Cold Calling and Professional Outreach.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: A professional introduction identifies the broker, explains a relevant capability and requests a brief conversation rather than reciting an elaborate sales pitch. Research the prospect's business, use accurate claims, honor opt-out requests and follow applicable marketing rules. Ask a specific service-oriented question.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A concise opening might be: 'I arrange dry van freight from northern Illinois into Texas. Are you the person responsible for outbound transportation, or is there someone else I should contact?' If the shipper says the current provider is adequate, offer a meaningful lane-specific reason to speak again instead of arguing.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know

video_storyboard.narration: Discovery focuses on lane origins and destinations, weekly volume, seasonality, freight characteristics, pickup and delivery windows, billing requirements, reporting expectations and common failures. video_storyboard.narration: A shipper says its current provider often misses a Wednesday delivery appointment. video_storyboard.narration: Send a concise recap of the shipper's stated needs, agreed next step, and quote assumptions. video_storyboard.narration: Find capacity by equipment, origin market, destination preference and schedule. video_storyboard.narration: Review FMCSA information for operating authority status, legal name and registration identifiers. video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A caller provides a carrier MC number but the legal name differs from the party named in its rate request. Stop booking and independently confirm the registration and authorized contact. Do not dismiss discrepancies as mere clerical errors without verification.

video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Verifying Carrier Identity and Insurance.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Fraud prevention requires independent callbacks using trustworthy contact sources, not telephone numbers supplied in a suspicious email. Verify operating authority, policy details and coverage adequacy for the particular commodity. Certificates alone are not definitive proof of an active policy; confirm through appropriate channels.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A new dispatcher asks you to replace the approved carrier's email address immediately before pickup and sends an updated certificate. video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Carrier onboarding collects the legal entity's registration identifiers, tax documentation, agreement acceptance, authorized dispatch contact, insurance evidence and verified remittance instructions. video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A carrier sends a signed agreement and asks to be paid into an account whose owner name differs from the carrier's legal entity. video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Preventing Carrier Fraud and Double Brokering.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Identity theft and unauthorized rebrokering can redirect a shipment to an unapproved party. video_storyboard.heading: Booking and Dispatching Your First Load
video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Booking and Dispatching Your First Load.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Booking is complete only after the carrier is screened, price and equipment agreed, instructions acknowledged and pickup details communicated. video_storyboard.narration: A load shows as 'in transit' but no pickup confirmation exists. Treat the status as unverified and call the approved carrier using a trusted contact. Confirm pickup date, seal/reference details and ETA before telling the customer the freight moved.

video_storyboard.narration: Appointments depend on facility hours, transit time, loading/unloading practices, route restrictions and the carrier's legal driving plan. video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A shipper in Chicago releases freight at 4 p.m. and a receiver in Dallas offers an 8 a.m. next-day appointment. Before agreeing, check distance, traffic, driver availability and hours-of-service limits with the carrier. Change the commitment if the timing is infeasible.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Track actual events, not just planned milestones. Record arrival at pickup, loading complete, departure, location or ETA updates, arrival at delivery, unloading and POD. video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A driver estimates delivery at noon, two hours after the appointment. Tell the shipper and receiver what is known, when the ETA will be reconfirmed and who is coordinating a new appointment. Keep the message factual and avoid blaming the carrier prematurely.

video_storyboard.narration: When problems occur, prioritize safety, facts, mitigation and documentation. video_storyboard.narration: A delivered load is not financially complete until POD, rate confirmation, carrier charges and customer billing are reconciled. video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow

video_storyboard.narration: Customer billing should match the accepted sell rate and documented, approved accessorials. Include the correct customer name, invoice number, load reference, service dates and payment terms; attach the POD or other agreed supporting records. An inaccurate invoice can delay collections and damage trust.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A $2,400 freight quote includes one pickup and one delivery. The carrier later requests a $100 additional-stop fee. Do not bill the shipper automatically; determine whether the second stop was ordered and approved under the agreed terms.

video_storyboard.narration: Reconcile the carrier invoice to the signed rate confirmation, agreed accessorials and proof of delivery. Check whether the carrier assigned payment to a factor. video_storyboard.narration: Credit analysis protects against shippers who cannot or will not pay on time. Factoring can accelerate cash receipts in exchange for a fee and contractual conditions, but it changes economics and administrative workflow. Distinguish a shipper's credit assessment from a carrier's factoring assignment.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example

video_storyboard.narration: A brokerage sells $10,000 of receivables to a factor for a hypothetical 3% fee, yielding $9,700 before any other adjustments. That fee affects net economics and should not be treated as freight transportation cost without a consistent accounting policy.

video_storyboard.visual: Freight logistics title card, dark navy and gold
video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Tracking Revenue, Margin and Cash Flow.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Measure revenue, carrier cost, gross profit, gross margin and overhead separately. Cash flow follows actual collection and payment timing, not the booking date. Use per-load profitability and aging reports to reveal accounts that consume capacity while creating little value.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: Three loads each sell for $2,500. If carrier costs are $2,000, $2,200 and $2,450, gross profits are $500, $300 and $50. The third load creates revenue but leaves little room for operating expenses or problems.

video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Building Financial Controls.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Define who can approve carrier onboarding, rate changes, customer credit and payment instructions. Segregate duties when practical and create an auditable exception log. video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Brokers face exposures from failed service, unauthorized carriers, fraud, cargo damage, unpaid charges and poorly drafted contracts. Not every risk is covered by the same insurance. Review the actual agreement and insurance terms with qualified advisers rather than promising blanket protection.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A cargo loss occurs after a motor carrier made an unapproved equipment substitution. video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: At delivery, document damaged packaging, shortage counts, seal discrepancies and any notation on the POD. Preserve photographs, invoices, shipping papers, communications and timestamps. Notify the carrier, shipper and insurers as appropriate; do not make admissions or promises of payment without authority.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: The consignee signs the POD noting three crushed cartons. Ask for clear photographs, the value of affected goods, shipment identifiers and records of loading condition. Keep the affected parties informed and follow applicable notice and claim procedures.

video_storyboard.narration: Welcome to Preventing Fraud and Cybercrime.

video_storyboard.heading: What you need to know
video_storyboard.visual: Concept diagram or operational example
video_storyboard.narration: Brokers are targets for phishing, fake carrier profiles, credential theft and fraudulent pickups. Require multifactor authentication, least-privilege access, independently verified changes and clear incident procedures. Stop a suspicious shipment before pickup whenever reasonable; recovery becomes harder once freight leaves a facility.

video_storyboard.heading: Worked freight example
video_storyboard.visual: Shipment, carrier, shipper and equipment workflow
video_storyboard.narration: A message resembling your load board provider asks you to sign in through a shortened link. Instead of clicking, open the known service site directly and verify the notice through official support. Reset credentials and report the event if staff entered information.

video_storyboard.narration: Unauthorized rebrokering occurs when a party transfers transportation arrangements without the required approval or authority. Use explicit consent and written records; do not let an intermediary conceal the actual motor carrier.

video_storyboard.narration: Resolve disputes with a shared timeline, documents and the contractual standard. Separate observed facts from opinions, identify the disputed amount or service condition and offer a written resolution process. Avoid escalating by blaming parties before investigating.

video_storyboard.narration: A practical risk plan assigns prevention controls, early warning signs, escalation owners, emergency contacts, evidence retention and periodic review. video_storyboard.narration: A transportation management system manages loads, documents and events; a CRM manages prospects and customers; accounting software handles invoices, payables and financial reporting. video_storyboard.narration: AI can draft messages, summarize carrier conversations and classify documents, but it can invent rates, identities or contractual terms.
